text: What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the head of a singly linked list when the head pointer is available?
explanation: Only the new node and head pointer need to be updated; the list does not need to be traversed.

text: Which data structure is typically used by breadth-first search to visit vertices level by level?
explanation: BFS processes discovered vertices in first-in, first-out order, which a queue provides.

text: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly selects the smallest remaining element and places it at the next position?
explanation: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum item in the unsorted suffix and swaps it into place.

text: In a binary search tree with distinct keys, which property holds for every node?
options: Every node has exactly two children
Keys in the left subtree are smaller and those in the right subtree are larger
explanation: The binary search tree ordering property places smaller keys left and larger keys right of each node.

text: For a well-distributed hash table with controlled load factor, what is the expected time complexity of lookup?
explanation: Hash lookup is expected constant time under suitable hashing and load-factor assumptions; worst-case collisions can be linear.

text: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort on an array of n elements?
explanation: Merge sort divides the input into logarithmic levels and performs linear merging work at each level.

text: For an unweighted graph, which algorithm finds a shortest path in number of edges from a source to every reachable vertex?
explanation: BFS explores vertices by increasing distance in edges, so the first discovery of a vertex gives a shortest unweighted path.

text: A stable sorting algorithm guarantees what?
options: It always uses O(1) extra memory
Equal-key items retain their original relative order
It is always faster than an unstable sort
It sorts data without comparisons in every case
explanation: Stability preserves the relative order of records whose sort keys compare equal.

text: Floyd’s tortoise-and-hare algorithm detects a cycle in a linked list using which time and extra-space bounds?
options: O(n) time and O(1) extra space
O(log n) time and O(n) extra space
O(n squared) time and O(1) extra space
O(1) time and O(n) extra space
explanation: Two pointers moving at different speeds can meet inside a cycle; the algorithm takes linear time and constant extra space.

text: Which property is a common reason a problem can benefit from dynamic programming?
options: The answer must be a graph
explanation: Dynamic programming reuses solutions to repeated subproblems and combines them according to an optimal-substructure relationship.

text: After building a binary max-heap, what is the worst-case time complexity of extracting its maximum element once?
explanation: The root maximum is removed, the last element replaces it, and heapify travels at most the tree height, which is logarithmic.

text: What is the worst-case time complexity of standard quicksort when each pivot repeatedly creates highly unbalanced partitions?
explanation: Repeated partitions of sizes 0 and n−1 yield quadratic work across recursive calls.

text: Dijkstra’s shortest-path algorithm relies on which important condition about edge weights?
options: The graph must be a tree
explanation: Dijkstra finalizes vertices greedily and is correct with non-negative edge weights; negative edges can invalidate that choice.

text: A topological ordering exists for which type of directed graph?
explanation: A DAG admits a linear ordering in which each directed edge points forward; a directed cycle makes such an order impossible.

text: What is the main purpose of a foreign key constraint?
options: To enforce a relationship to a referenced key
To guarantee every query uses an index
explanation: A foreign key enforces referential integrity between related tables.

text: In SQL, what does COUNT(*) count?
options: Only rows where every column is non-NULL
All rows in the selected group or result
Only rows with a numeric primary key
explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULL values in individual columns.

text: Which ACID property means that committed changes survive a subsequent system failure, subject to the database’s durability guarantees?
explanation: Durability requires committed transaction results to persist beyond the transaction and survive supported failures.

text: Which normal-form principle requires each table cell to contain a single value from its domain rather than a repeating list of values?
explanation: First normal form requires attributes to contain atomic values and rows to be structured without repeating groups.

text: What is a non-repeatable read?
options: A transaction reads the same row twice and sees different committed values
A table has no primary key
A transaction writes the same value twice within one statement
explanation: A concurrent transaction updates a row between two reads, so the first transaction observes different values.

text: Why can adding an index slow down INSERT and UPDATE operations?
options: The database may also need to maintain the index entries
Every write must scan the entire database by definition
explanation: Index maintenance adds work and storage to writes, though indexes can make some reads much faster.

text: Which problem occurs when two transactions overwrite each other’s changes because each read an older value?
explanation: A lost update occurs when one transaction’s write unintentionally replaces another transaction’s update.

text: If A functionally determines B, written A → B, what does that mean?
options: Each value of A is associated with one value of B in the relation
A and B must be primary keys
A and B must contain identical values
explanation: A → B means rows agreeing on A must agree on B.

text: What is a dirty read?
options: Reading data written by a transaction that has not committed
Reading a row twice after it committed
explanation: A dirty read exposes another transaction’s uncommitted changes, which might later be rolled back.

text: Which index is most likely to help a query filtering on the leading column of a composite index (A, B)?
options: An index on unrelated column C only
No index can help a leading-column filter
An index only on B always replaces it
explanation: Many database engines can use the leftmost prefix of a composite index, including a predicate on A alone.

text: Which anomaly involves a transaction rerunning a range query and finding new rows inserted by another committed transaction?
explanation: A phantom read occurs when repeating a predicate-based query returns a different set of rows due to concurrent inserts or deletes.

text: Which standard isolation level is intended to make concurrent transactions behave as if they executed in some serial order?
explanation: Serializable is the isolation level defined to provide serializable transaction behavior, though implementations use different techniques.

text: What is a common trade-off of a B-tree index on a frequently updated table?
options: Faster qualifying reads at the cost of storage and index-maintenance work
It eliminates the need for constraints
explanation: B-tree indexes are useful for many equality and range predicates but consume storage and add work to writes.

text: Why should an application avoid assuming that a transaction will always be retried safely after a network timeout?
options: A timeout proves that the transaction rolled back
The transaction might have committed even if the client did not receive the response
A retry always deletes the database
explanation: After a lost response the client may not know whether the server committed; idempotency keys or outcome checks help avoid duplicate effects.

text: What is a typical purpose of user mode in an operating system?
options: Restrict applications from executing privileged operations directly
explanation: User mode limits privileges so applications must request protected operations through controlled kernel interfaces.

text: What information is commonly stored in a process control block?
options: Process state, scheduling information and saved execution context
explanation: The PCB holds operating-system bookkeeping needed to manage and resume a process.

text: What does virtual memory allow an operating system to provide?
options: An address space abstraction that can exceed or differ from physical RAM layout
A guarantee that programs never use disk
explanation: Virtual memory maps process addresses to physical memory and may use secondary storage to support address spaces larger than resident RAM.

text: What is a race condition?
options: A condition where output depends on the timing or interleaving of concurrent operations
A process with a high CPU frequency
A queue sorted by arrival time
A network packet sent twice by definition
explanation: Unsynchronised concurrent accesses can produce results that depend on execution interleavings.

text: What is a context switch?
options: Saving one execution context and restoring another so the CPU can run different work
Converting a process into a file
explanation: The OS saves state for the currently scheduled task and restores state for another task.

text: What is the principal role of a mutex?
options: To provide mutual exclusion around a shared resource
To guarantee deadlock can never occur
explanation: A mutex permits controlled exclusive access to a critical section, though incorrect lock ordering can still cause deadlocks.

text: A counting semaphore initialised to 3 is often used to represent what?
options: Up to three units of a resource may be acquired simultaneously
A process must execute three times
explanation: A counting semaphore tracks a quantity of available permits for a limited resource pool.

text: What is thrashing in a virtual-memory system?
options: A CPU instruction changing arithmetic signs
Excessive paging that leaves little time for useful execution
explanation: Thrashing occurs when memory pressure causes frequent page faults and paging activity that overwhelm useful work.

text: What is starvation in process scheduling?
options: A process waits indefinitely because other work repeatedly receives the needed resource or CPU
A process consumes exactly zero memory
explanation: Starvation is indefinite postponement; fair scheduling or aging can reduce it.

text: With demand paging, when can a page be brought into physical memory?
options: Only when the operating system starts
When the process first accesses it and the page is not resident
Only when a file is deleted
Every clock cycle regardless of access
explanation: A page fault can trigger loading a page on first access or when it has been evicted from RAM.

text: What does the Banker’s algorithm attempt to determine before granting a resource request?
options: Whether the resulting state is safe according to declared resource needs
Whether the process source code compiles
Whether every process uses one thread
Whether the disk is full only
explanation: Banker’s algorithm grants requests only if the resulting state admits a safe sequence for processes to finish.

text: Why can shortest-job-first scheduling minimise average waiting time under its classical assumptions?
options: It runs the longest jobs first
Short jobs complete earlier and add less waiting to the queue when burst lengths are known
It guarantees no starvation in all variants
explanation: With known CPU burst lengths and comparable jobs, running the shortest remaining burst first reduces average waiting time; long jobs can still starve.

text: What is a page table used for?
options: Mapping virtual page numbers to physical frames and recording related status bits
explanation: Page tables hold mappings and permission/status information used by address translation.

text: Why is a deadlock prevention strategy based on resource ordering effective?
options: It ensures every process receives every resource instantly
It can break circular wait by requiring locks to be acquired in a global order
It makes processes run only in user mode
explanation: A consistent global resource ordering prevents cycles in the resource-allocation graph, breaking the circular-wait condition.

text: On a typical IPv4 local network, what does ARP help a host discover?
options: The MAC address associated with a local IPv4 address
explanation: ARP resolves a local IPv4 next-hop address to a link-layer hardware address.

text: Which transport protocol is connectionless and does not itself guarantee delivery or ordering?
explanation: UDP provides datagrams without TCP-style connection setup, retransmission or ordered delivery guarantees.

text: What is the usual role of DHCP on a client network?
options: Assign configuration such as an IP address and default gateway
explanation: DHCP can lease IP configuration and related settings to hosts automatically.

text: What does TLS primarily provide for a network connection when correctly configured?
options: Encryption in transit and integrity, with server authentication in common web use
Automatic protection from every application bug
An IP address for every device
explanation: TLS protects data in transit and supports authenticated connections; it does not fix every endpoint vulnerability.

text: How many traditionally usable host addresses are in an IPv4 /26 subnet?
explanation: A /26 leaves 6 host bits, giving 64 addresses; excluding network and broadcast leaves 62 traditionally usable host addresses.

text: What does a router primarily use its routing table for?
options: To choose a next hop or outgoing interface for an IP packet
explanation: Routing-table entries help determine how to forward packets toward destination IP networks.

text: What is a common purpose of network address translation (NAT) in home IPv4 networks?
options: Allow multiple private-address devices to share a public IPv4 address for outbound access
explanation: Many home gateways translate private source addresses and ports to a shared public address.

text: What is the main purpose of TCP sequence numbers and acknowledgements?
options: Support ordered delivery and identify received byte ranges
explanation: Sequence numbers identify bytes and acknowledgements communicate received data, enabling ordered reliable delivery.

text: What is network congestion control intended to do?
options: Adjust sending behavior to reduce overload within the network
explanation: Congestion control adapts traffic to network conditions to avoid overwhelming bottlenecks.

text: Which protocol is commonly used to resolve a domain name to address records?
explanation: DNS resolves domain names and can return A, AAAA and other record types.

text: Why can TCP retransmit a segment even when the original segment may have reached the receiver?
options: The acknowledgement may have been lost or delayed
The receiver must always delete received bytes
The IP address changed in every case
explanation: If an acknowledgement does not arrive before the retransmission logic triggers, TCP may resend data even if the receiver got the original.

text: How long is an IPv6 address?
explanation: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, offering a much larger address space than IPv4.

text: A Layer 2 Ethernet switch normally learns which information to help forward unicast frames?
options: Source MAC addresses and the ports where they were observed
explanation: A learning switch builds a MAC address table from source MAC addresses and ingress ports.

text: What is a key difference between link-layer error detection and end-to-end transport reliability?
options: A link-layer checksum or CRC detects some errors on a link but does not alone guarantee end-to-end delivery
Transport reliability works only on one Ethernet cable
explanation: Link-layer checks detect certain transmission errors locally; delivery, ordering and retransmission end to end require higher-layer mechanisms where provided.

text: What is abstraction in object-oriented design?
options: Exposing essential behaviour while hiding unnecessary implementation details
Copying every field into every object
Sorting all objects by memory address
Removing all methods from a class
explanation: Abstraction presents a useful contract while hiding internal details not needed by the caller.

text: What is a constructor commonly used for when an object is created?
explanation: A constructor establishes the initial valid state of a new object.

text: What is the goal of access modifiers such as private and public?
options: Control which code can access a class member
Change an integer into a string automatically
explanation: Access modifiers control visibility and help enforce encapsulation boundaries.

text: What relationship is usually modelled by class inheritance?
options: An “is-a” relationship where a subtype can be used as its base type under the contract
A process waiting for a lock
explanation: Inheritance models a subtype relationship when substitutability and design semantics are appropriate.

text: In a language with dynamic dispatch, what usually determines which overridden instance method implementation is called?
options: The order of files on disk only
explanation: Dynamic dispatch selects an implementation based on the runtime type of the receiver.

text: Why might composition be preferred over inheritance for sharing behaviour between unrelated classes?
options: It allows behavior to be assembled through contained collaborators with looser coupling
It automatically makes all fields public
It always uses less memory in every language
explanation: Composition allows a class to delegate to collaborators without creating a rigid subtype relationship.

text: What is the primary purpose of an interface or protocol in object-oriented design?
options: Specify operations that implementing types agree to provide
Force every implementation to use identical internal code
explanation: Interfaces define a contract independent of the implementation details.

text: What is method overloading in languages that support it?
options: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter signatures
Replacing a method in a subclass only
explanation: Overloading selects among same-named methods based on their parameter lists according to language rules.

text: What is a benefit of an immutable object?
options: Its state cannot be changed after construction, which can simplify reasoning about sharing
It can never be passed to a function
explanation: Stable state reduces unexpected side effects and can simplify concurrent use.

text: The Liskov substitution principle says that a well-designed subtype should do what?
options: Be usable where its base type is expected without breaking the base type’s behavioural contract
Only be created with static methods
explanation: Subtypes should preserve the behavioural expectations of their base abstractions.

text: In Java, can a static method be overridden with runtime polymorphic dispatch in the same way as an instance method?
options: No; static methods are hidden rather than dynamically overridden
Only if the method returns void
Only when the class has no constructor
explanation: Static methods are associated with the class and are resolved by hiding rules rather than runtime instance dispatch.

text: A subtype strengthens a method’s precondition so it rejects some inputs accepted by the base class. Which principle may this violate?
explanation: Strengthening preconditions can break callers that were valid under the base-class contract, violating substitutability.

text: What does the dependency inversion principle recommend for high-level policy and low-level details?
options: Both should depend on abstractions rather than high-level policy depending directly on low-level details
High-level code must import every concrete class directly
All modules must be global variables
Low-level modules must control business policy
explanation: Dependency inversion places abstractions between high-level policy and implementation details.

text: Why should a constructor avoid exposing a partially initialised object before validation completes?
options: Other code could observe an object that violates its invariants
It prevents garbage collection from ever running
explanation: Publishing a partially initialised object can let other code observe invalid state or invoke methods before invariants hold.

text: Which SQL clause filters groups after GROUP BY aggregation?
explanation: HAVING filters grouped results, often using aggregate expressions; WHERE filters rows before grouping.

text: Which SQL expression returns the first non-NULL value from its arguments in databases that support it?
explanation: COALESCE evaluates arguments from left to right and returns the first non-NULL value.

text: What does UNION ALL do when combining compatible SELECT results?
options: Sorts every row by primary key
explanation: UNION ALL concatenates result rows without duplicate elimination.

text: Which SQL command usually makes the current transaction’s changes permanent?
explanation: COMMIT completes the transaction and makes its changes durable according to the database guarantees.

text: What distinguishes a window function from an ordinary aggregate that groups rows?
options: It can calculate across a related set of rows while keeping each input row in the result
It always deletes rows after calculation
It can only return one row total
explanation: Window functions compute over partitions or frames while retaining row-level output.

text: Which window function assigns the same rank to ties and leaves gaps in the following rank numbers?
explanation: RANK gives tied rows the same rank and leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not leave gaps.

text: What is a correlated subquery?
options: A subquery that references columns from its outer query
A query with no FROM clause only
A query that must create a new database
A query that can only return integers
explanation: A correlated subquery uses values from the surrounding query and is logically evaluated in that outer-row context.

text: Which join returns matching rows from both inputs and omits rows without a match?
explanation: An inner join includes only rows satisfying the join condition.

text: What is the strongest general approach for passing user-supplied values into SQL queries?
options: Concatenate raw input into SQL text
Use parameterised queries or prepared statements
Remove spaces from the input only
explanation: Parameterised queries keep values separate from query syntax and help prevent SQL injection.

text: Why might an index not improve a query that returns most rows in a table?
options: A full scan may be cheaper than many index lookups and table reads
Indexes cannot store any key values
SQL ignores all indexes for SELECT
An index always makes the query invalid
explanation: For low-selectivity predicates, scanning the table can cost less than traversing an index and fetching a large fraction of rows.

text: What is a common use of a recursive common table expression (CTE)?
options: Traverse hierarchical or graph-like relationships such as an organisational tree
Guarantee all queries run in constant time
explanation: Recursive CTEs repeatedly apply a query to prior results, which supports hierarchy and reachability queries.

text: What requirement generally applies to the SELECT statements combined with UNION?
options: They must return the same number of columns with compatible corresponding types
They must query the same physical table
They must use identical WHERE clauses
Each must return exactly one row
explanation: Set operations combine corresponding columns, so both branches must have compatible result shapes and types.

text: What is a key difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE in many relational databases?
options: DELETE can filter individual rows with WHERE; TRUNCATE generally removes all rows as a bulk operation
TRUNCATE is always identical across all database products
explanation: DELETE supports row predicates; TRUNCATE is typically a bulk table operation with database-specific transactional and identity behavior.

text: Why should an application use a unique idempotency key for a retryable payment-like operation?
options: To identify repeated submissions as the same logical operation and avoid duplicate effects
To make the SQL query always return NULL
To expose all internal error details
explanation: A stable idempotency key lets the application detect duplicate requests when the client retries after an uncertain response.

text: A product priced at 800 receives a 25% discount. What is the discounted price?
explanation: A 25% discount is 200, so the discounted price is 800 − 200 = 600.

text: What is the arithmetic mean of 4, 8, and 12?
A vehicle travels 120 km in 2 hours at a constant speed. What is its speed?
explanation: Speed is distance divided by time: 120 / 2 = 60 km/h.

text: What is the simple interest on 1000 at 5% per year for 2 years?
explanation: Simple interest is P × r × t = 1000 × 0.05 × 2 = 100.

text: A can complete a job in 6 days and B can complete the same job in 3 days. If their rates add, how long do they take working together?
explanation: Their combined daily rate is 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the job, so the job takes 2 days.

text: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
explanation: The favourable outcomes are 5 and 6, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

text: A mixture contains water and juice in the ratio 2:3. If the mixture is 25 litres, how many litres are juice?
explanation: There are five total parts, and juice is three parts: 25 × 3/5 = 15 litres.

text: A quantity increases from 80 to 100. What is the percentage increase?
explanation: The increase is 20, and 20/80 × 100% = 25%.

text: How many ways can a committee of 2 be chosen from 5 distinct people, ignoring order?
explanation: The number of combinations is 5 choose 2 = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10.

text: Two trains move toward each other at 50 km/h and 70 km/h. What is their closing speed?
explanation: When objects move toward each other, their closing speed is the sum: 50 + 70 = 120 km/h.

text: What is the amount on 1000 after 2 years at 10% annual compound interest, compounded yearly?
explanation: The amount is 1000 × 1.1² = 1210.

text: How many distinct arrangements are possible for the letters A, B, C, and D if each letter is used exactly once?
explanation: Four distinct items can be ordered in 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways.

text: A pipe fills a tank in 4 hours while a leak empties a full tank in 12 hours. If both operate together from empty, how long to fill the tank?
explanation: Net filling rate is 1/4 − 1/12 = 1/6 tank per hour, so filling takes 6 hours.

text: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
explanation: The probability is (3/5) × (2/4) = 6/20 = 3/10.

text: What is an important property expected of an idempotent HTTP method such as PUT?
options: Repeating the same request has the same intended effect as making it once
It must never carry a request body
It can only be sent over HTTP without TLS
explanation: Idempotence concerns intended server effect, not necessarily identical response codes or bodies.

text: What does HTTP status 201 Created normally communicate?
options: The server encountered a syntax error
explanation: 201 indicates that the request resulted in creation of a resource.

text: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute prevent?
options: Client-side JavaScript from reading the cookie through browser cookie APIs
The browser from sending the cookie to the server
The server from setting the cookie over HTTPS
explanation: HttpOnly prevents direct access to that cookie from client-side scripts, though it does not by itself prevent every XSS impact.

text: In event bubbling, after an event occurs on a nested element, where can it propagate next?
options: Toward ancestor elements in the DOM tree
Only to elements with no parents
explanation: Bubbling propagates an event from the target through its ancestors unless propagation is stopped.

text: Which HTTP method is conventionally used to retrieve a representation without requesting a state-changing action?
explanation: GET is defined for retrieval and is intended to be safe; applications should not use it for state-changing actions.

text: What security issue is a SameSite cookie attribute primarily designed to help mitigate?
options: Cross-site request forgery risks from cross-site cookie sending
explanation: SameSite can limit cross-site cookie attachment and therefore helps reduce CSRF exposure, but it is not a complete CSRF strategy in every setup.

text: What is reflected cross-site scripting (XSS)?
options: Untrusted input is included in a response and interpreted as executable script by a browser
A request is cached for too long
A server returns a correct JSON document
explanation: Reflected XSS occurs when attacker-controlled input is reflected into a page without appropriate context-sensitive output encoding or sanitisation.

text: What does Promise.all normally do when one of its input promises rejects?
options: The combined promise rejects with that failure, while other operations may still be running
It silently converts every rejection into success
It cancels all underlying network requests automatically
It waits forever and never settles
explanation: Promise.all rejects when an input rejects; it does not automatically cancel the other underlying tasks.

text: Why use semantic HTML elements such as main, nav, and button instead of generic div elements everywhere?
options: They communicate structure and interaction semantics to browsers and assistive technologies
They automatically prevent all security vulnerabilities
They remove the need for CSS
explanation: Semantic elements provide meaningful structure and native behavior that can improve accessibility and maintainability.

text: What is the main purpose of a Content Security Policy (CSP)?
options: Restrict which resource sources and execution behaviors a browser should allow
explanation: CSP is a browser-enforced policy that can limit resource loading and script execution, reducing the impact of some injection attacks.

text: Why does a CSRF attack commonly exploit a browser’s automatic inclusion of credentials such as cookies?
options: A victim’s browser may send authenticated cookies with a forged cross-site request
The attacker must know the victim’s password in plaintext
explanation: Cookie-based ambient credentials can accompany forged requests; SameSite, CSRF tokens, origin checks and suitable API design help mitigate it.

text: A browser sends a CORS preflight request using OPTIONS. What is the browser generally checking?
options: Whether the server permits the requested origin, method and headers for the upcoming cross-origin request
Whether the user’s password has expired
Whether the response HTML contains a title
explanation: Preflight lets the browser ask whether a server allows the proposed cross-origin method and headers.

text: Why is localStorage generally unsuitable for storing a long-lived bearer access token in an XSS-sensitive application?
options: JavaScript running in the origin can read it if script execution is compromised
It expires every second by specification
The server cannot accept bearer tokens
explanation: Origin JavaScript can access localStorage, so an XSS payload can potentially exfiltrate stored tokens; in-memory access tokens reduce persistence exposure.

text: What is the conventional distinction between HTTP 401 and 403?
options: 401 indicates missing or invalid authentication; 403 indicates the server refuses access despite understanding the request, often after authentication
401 means database full; 403 means network cable unplugged
They always mean exactly the same thing
explanation: 401 is associated with missing or invalid authentication credentials; 403 indicates refusal to fulfil an understood request.

text: What is data leakage in machine learning evaluation?
options: Information unavailable at prediction time improperly influences training or evaluation
The dataset contains any missing values
explanation: Leakage occurs when training or evaluation uses information that would not legitimately be available for the intended prediction.

text: What is a common goal of regularisation?
options: Reduce overfitting by discouraging unnecessarily complex model behavior
Increase the number of duplicate examples
Remove the need for a validation set
explanation: Regularisation penalises or constrains model complexity to improve generalisation.

text: Recall for the positive class is defined as which ratio?
explanation: Recall measures the share of actual positive examples correctly identified.

text: What is the output of ReLU for a negative input x?
explanation: ReLU is max(0, x), so negative inputs map to zero.

text: Why is cross-validation often used when evaluating a model on a limited dataset?
options: It measures performance across multiple train-validation splits rather than relying on one split alone
It guarantees that data leakage is impossible
It increases the dataset with new ground truth
It removes the need for a final held-out test set in every project
explanation: Cross-validation provides a more stable estimate by rotating validation folds; a final held-out test set can still be useful.

text: Why should a standard scaler be fitted only on the training split and then applied to validation and test splits?
options: To avoid leaking information from evaluation data into preprocessing parameters
To make all target labels equal
To improve a model by changing test labels
Because validation data cannot contain numbers
explanation: Means and standard deviations estimated on all data reveal information from evaluation samples; fit transformations only on training data.

text: What is the basic objective of k-means clustering?
options: Minimise within-cluster squared distances to the assigned cluster centroids
Maximise supervised classification accuracy using labels
Find a shortest path through a graph
Estimate only a linear regression slope
explanation: K-means alternates assignments and centroid updates to reduce within-cluster sum of squared distances.

text: A model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern and performs poorly on both train and test data. Which issue is most likely?
explanation: Underfitting commonly reflects high bias and poor fit even on training examples.

text: What does the learning rate control in gradient-based optimisation?
options: The step size used when updating parameters
The number of classes in the dataset
explanation: The learning rate scales parameter updates; overly high or low values can prevent effective optimisation.

text: Why can accuracy be misleading on a dataset where 99% of examples are negative?
options: A classifier predicting negative every time would achieve 99% accuracy while missing all positives
An imbalanced dataset cannot be evaluated
Accuracy is always smaller than recall
explanation: The majority class dominates accuracy, so minority-class recall, precision, PR-AUC and the confusion matrix may be important.

text: What does ROC-AUC measure in a binary classification setting?
options: The area under the true-positive-rate versus false-positive-rate curve across thresholds
explanation: ROC-AUC summarises ranking discrimination across thresholds through the ROC curve.

text: What is a primary effect of a convolutional layer in a CNN for images?
options: Apply learned local filters across spatial positions to detect patterns
Guarantee rotation invariance without any design or training considerations
Convert all pixels into class labels directly
explanation: Convolutional filters learn local patterns and are reused spatially; invariance depends on architecture, data and training.

text: In principal component analysis (PCA), the first principal component is the direction that, under standard PCA, does what?
options: Maximises variance of the projected data
Maximises the number of class labels
Guarantees the features become independent in every distribution
explanation: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance in centred data; it does not guarantee statistical independence generally.

text: When choosing a classification threshold for a real product, why should a team consider the relative cost of false positives and false negatives?
options: Different threshold choices trade precision against recall, and error costs vary by application
The threshold has no effect on predictions
The test set can be used repeatedly until the score looks best
False positives and false negatives are always equally harmful
explanation: Threshold choice changes the confusion matrix; selecting it should reflect application costs and usually be based on validation data.
